$$
A=[\begin{aligned}0 & -2 \\ 0 & 4 \\ 0 & 4\end{aligned}],\,Σ=[\begin{aligned}6 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices $A$ and $Σ$ shown above. Given that $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ which of the following could be the matrix $V?$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that if  $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of a $3\times 2$ matrix $A,$ then

- $Σ$ is a $3\times 2$ matrix with nonnegative elements on the main diagonal and zeroes outside the main diagonal,

- $U$ is an orthogonal $3\times 3$ matrix,

- $V$ is an orthogonal $2\times 2$ matrix.

Let's find the singular value decomposition of $A$ using the usual algorithm.

- **Step 1.** Compute ${A}^{T}\,A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A & ={[\begin{aligned}0 & -2 \\ 0 & 4 \\ 0 & 4\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}0 & -2 \\ 0 & 4 \\ 0 & 4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & 0 \\ -2 & 4 & 4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 & -2 \\ 0 & 4 \\ 0 & 4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 36\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

- **Step 2.** Find the singular values: From the matrix $Σ,$ we deduce that ${\sigma }_{1}=6$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=0.$

- **Step 3.** Find the right singular vectors of $A$ (i.e., the unit eigenvectors of ${A}^{T}\,A$):

- For ${\lambda }_{1}={\sigma }_{1}^{2}=36,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A-36I & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 36\end{aligned}]-36[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-36 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $({A}^{T}\,A-36I)v=0$ gives the unit eigenvector

$$
{v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}={\sigma }_{2}^{2}=0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A-0I & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 36\end{aligned}]-0[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 36\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $({A}^{T}\,A-0I)v=0$ gives the unit eigenvector

$$
{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, we construct the matrix $V:$

$$
V=[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}]
$$

-\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}{x}_{2}+\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}{x}_{3}=0\,⟹\,-{x}_{2}+2{x}_{3}=0,
$$

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ 2{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]={x}_{1}{{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{b}_{1}}+{x}_{3}{{[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{b}_{2}},
$$

where ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{3}$ are free variables.

Notice that the two linearly independent solutions ${b}_{1}$ and ${b}_{2}$ are mutually orthogonal. Therefore, we only need to normalize them. This gives the second and third columns of $U:$   

$$
{u}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\,{u}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\end{aligned}]
$$

$$
U=[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 0 \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} & 0 & \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} & 0 & \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\end{aligned}]
$$

questions.worked_solution:
Recall that if  $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of a $3\times 2$ matrix $A,$ then

- $Σ$ is a $3\times 2$ matrix with nonnegative elements on the main diagonal and zeroes outside the main diagonal,

- $U$ is an orthogonal $3\times 3$ matrix,

- $V$ is an orthogonal $2\times 2$ matrix.

From the matrix $Σ,$ we deduce that ${\sigma }_{1}=5\sqrt{2}$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=0.$
Also, the columns ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ of $V$ give us the right singular vectors of $A.$

Therefore, we can compute the first column of $U$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{1}}A{v}_{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{5\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}4 & 0 \\ 5 & 0 \\ 3 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{5\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 5 \\ 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{4}{5\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{5}{5\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{3}{5\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

  

Since the second singular value is ${\sigma }_{2}=0$, and we do not have the third singular value, we can't use the same formula to find the second and third columns of $U.$ But we know that $U$ must be orthogonal. Hence, we must find vectors 

$$
u=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]
$$

such that ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0$ and $‖u‖=1.$

Solving ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0,$ which is equivalent to

$$
\frac{4}{5\sqrt{2}}{x}_{1}+\frac{5}{5\sqrt{2}}{x}_{2}+\frac{3}{5\sqrt{2}}{x}_{3}=0\,⟹\,4{x}_{1}+5{x}_{2}+3{x}_{3}=0,
$$

we get the general solution 

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ -\frac{4}{3}{x}_{1}-\frac{5}{3}{x}_{2}\end{aligned}]=\frac{1}{3}{x}_{1}{{[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 0 \\ -4\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{b}_{1}}+\frac{1}{3}{x}_{2}{{[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 3 \\ -5\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{b}_{2}},
$$

where ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}$ are free variables. 

Notice that the two linearly independent solutions ${b}_{1}$ and ${b}_{2}$ are *not* mutually orthogonal. Therefore, we have to orthogonalize them using the Gram-Schmidt process. So, let 

$$
{c}_{1}={b}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 0 \\ -4\end{aligned}].
$$

Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}{c}_{2} & ={b}_{2}-\frac{{b}_{2}\cdot {c}_{1}}{{c}_{1}\cdot {c}_{1}}{c}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 3 \\ -5\end{aligned}]-\frac{20}{25}[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 0 \\ -4\end{aligned}]=\frac{3}{5}[\begin{aligned}-4 \\ 5 \\ -3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, normalizing orthogonal vectors ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2},$ we obtain the second and third columns of $U:$   

$$
{u}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{5} \\ 0 \\ -\frac{4}{5}\end{aligned}],\,{u}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{4}{5\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{5}{5\sqrt{2}} \\ -\frac{3}{5\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}]
$$

So, the matrix $U$ could be the following:

$$
U=[\begin{aligned}\frac{4}{5\sqrt{2}} & \frac{3}{5} & -\frac{4}{5\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{5}{5\sqrt{2}} & 0 & \frac{5}{5\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{3}{5\sqrt{2}} & -\frac{4}{5} & -\frac{3}{5\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}]
$$
